items.figure: Draw a solenoid with the steel bar AB placed inside it, connected in series to a cell and a switch. Show the current around end A as anticlockwise when viewed from A; label A as N and B as S. (The current direction can be reversed by reversing the cell connections.)
steps: Draw a solenoid with the steel bar AB inside it and connect the solenoid, a cell and a switch in series.
Choose the current direction so that, when viewed from end A, the current around the solenoid is anticlockwise.
By the right-hand grip rule, this makes end A a north pole and end B a south pole.
items.finalAnswer: The diagram shows a steel bar inside a solenoid connected to a cell and switch, with A as N and B as S.

items.figure: Draw two bar magnets symmetrically with like poles facing across the gap; for example, label the facing ends N and N and the two outer ends S. Draw field lines emerging from both facing N poles and bending away from the middle, with equal and opposite field directions at the midpoint. Place a compass at the midpoint and show its needle along the north-south direction.
steps: The poles facing each other must be like poles (N–N or S–S).
At the middle of the gap, the magnetic fields due to the two magnets are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so they cancel.
With no resultant field from the magnets at the midpoint, the compass needle settles in the north-south direction under the influence of Earth’s magnetic field.
items.finalAnswer: Like poles face each other, so their magnetic fields cancel at the midpoint and the compass aligns north-south.

steps: Yes. A changing magnetic field can produce an electric current in a conductor. This phenomenon is called electromagnetic induction.
For example, connect a coil to a galvanometer and move a bar magnet into or out of the coil.
The galvanometer shows a deflection while the magnet is moving, indicating that a current is induced in the coil.
The current is produced only while the magnetic field through the coil is changing.
items.finalAnswer: Yes; a changing magnetic field induces current, as when a magnet is moved into or out of a coil.

items.figure: Draw four solenoids symmetrically around O, with their axes directed radially. Label the ends facing O as N and the outer ends as S for all four solenoids. Show equal currents, each anticlockwise when viewed from O at the inner end. Indicate that if any one solenoid is switched off, the resultant field at O points toward its position.
steps: Make the ends of all four solenoids facing O north poles, with the same current magnitude in each.
By the right-hand grip rule, show the current in each solenoid anticlockwise when viewed from O at its inner end.
The field at O due to each solenoid is directed away from that solenoid. With all four operating, these equal radial fields cancel in opposite pairs.

If one solenoid is switched off, the other three fields no longer cancel. Their resultant is opposite to the field that the switched-off solenoid would have produced, so it is directed towards that solenoid.
items.finalAnswer: Make every end facing O a north pole; when any one solenoid is switched off, the resultant field at O points towards it.

steps: Bring one pole of a known magnet near the object.
Repulsion proves that the object is a magnet, because repulsion occurs only between like poles of two magnets.
Attraction alone does not prove that the object is a magnet, because a magnet also attracts magnetic materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt.
items.finalAnswer: Use the repulsion test: repulsion proves the object is a magnet; attraction alone does not.

items.figure: Draw: (1) a bar magnet with field lines close together near its poles and farther apart away from them; (2) a uniform magnetic field represented by straight, parallel, equally spaced lines; (3) a weaker field represented by lines farther apart. Add arrows showing the direction of the field lines, from N to S outside a magnet.
steps: The strength of a magnetic field is represented by the closeness of its magnetic lines of force.
Where the lines are close together, the magnetic field is strong; where they are farther apart, the field is weak.
A uniform magnetic field is shown by straight, parallel, equally spaced lines.
Around a bar magnet, the lines are most crowded near the poles, so the field is strongest there.
items.finalAnswer: A magnetic field is stronger where its lines of force are closer together and weaker where they are farther apart.

items.figure: Draw a circuit with a circuit breaker in series with a load. Inside the breaker, show contacts held closed by a latch, an electromagnet in series, and an iron armature connected to the latch. Show an arrow indicating that excessive current makes the electromagnet pull the armature and open the contacts.
steps: A circuit breaker is a safety device that automatically breaks an electric circuit when the current becomes excessive.
It works on the magnetic effect of electric current. The current in the circuit passes through a coil in the breaker.
When the current becomes too large, the coil becomes a strong electromagnet and attracts an iron armature.
The armature releases the latch and opens the contacts, breaking the circuit and stopping the current.
After the fault is removed, the breaker can be reset.
items.finalAnswer: A circuit breaker automatically opens a circuit when excessive current makes its electromagnet release the contacts.

steps: The statement is not correct if it means that a magnet attracts only another magnet.
A magnet also attracts magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt, even when they are not magnets.
Repulsion, however, occurs only between like poles of two magnets.
items.finalAnswer: A magnet attracts magnetic materials as well as magnets; repulsion is the sure test for identifying a magnet.
